source_text: Sed ut nunc nobis sermo de praesentibus sit, generatio proprie sexibus imputatur, imitatio autem semper animorum est. Hic ergo affectus animi, quod possibiliter voluerit imitantis, hominem pro diversitate causarum aut accusat, aut provehit; ita fit ut in bono et Deum, et Angelos, et Apostolos dicatur imitari; Deum: Estote perfecti, sicut Pater vester perfectus est [n61] ; Angelos: Fiat voluntas tua, sicut in caelo et in terra [n62] ; Apostolos: Imitatores mei estote, sicut et ego Christi [n63] . In malo vero imitatur diabolum, sicut dicitur: Imitantur eum, qui sunt ex parte ipsius [n64] ; imitantur homines: Nolite esse tristes sicut hypocritae, exterminantes facies suas [n65] , imitantur animalia, cum mandatur: Nolite fieri sicut equus et mulus, quibus non est intellectus [n66] . His ergo verbis, tam adhortantibus quam deterrentibus, ostenditur imitationis affectus, qui utique si esse non posset, non indiceretur cavendus.
pass_a_gloss: But that our speech may now be about present things, generation is properly imputed to the sexes, but imitation is always of souls. This affect of the mind, therefore, which the imitator has possibly willed, either accuses a human being according to the diversity of causes, or advances him; so it happens that in the good both God and Angels and Apostles are said to be imitated; God: Be perfect, as your Father is perfect; Angels: Your will be done, as in heaven also on earth; Apostles: Be imitators of me, as I also of Christ. But in the evil he imitates the devil, as it is said: They imitate him, who are from his party; they imitate human beings: Do not be sad as the hypocrites, destroying their faces; they imitate animals, when it is commanded: Do not become as a horse and a mule, to whom there is not understanding. By these words, therefore, both exhorting and deterring, the affect of imitation is shown, which certainly, if it could not be, would not be enjoined as to be guarded against.

pass_b_english: To keep our discussion on the matter at hand: generation properly concerns the sexes, while imitation always concerns minds. This disposition of a mind that imitates what it freely chooses either incriminates a person or advances him, according to the different circumstances. Thus, in good conduct, a person is said to imitate God, angels, and apostles. God: ‘Be perfect, as your Father is perfect’ (Matthew 5:48) (Psalm 32:9;). Angels: ‘Your will be done on earth as in heaven’ (Matthew 6:10). Apostles: ‘Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ’ (1 Corinthians 11:1). In evil conduct, however, a person imitates the devil, as Scripture says: ‘Those who belong to his party imitate him’ (Wisdom 2:24; Latin numbering 2:25). People imitate human beings: ‘Do not be gloomy like the hypocrites, disfiguring their faces’ (Matthew 6:16). They imitate animals, as in the command: ‘Do not become like a horse or mule, which have no understanding’ (Psalm 32:9; LXX/Vulgate 31:9). These words, whether encouraging or warning, show the disposition to imitate. If it were impossible, we certainly would not be told to guard against it.

choices.why: Julian's Rom 5:12 reading: sin passes by copying Adam's example, not by generation/seed.
Julian's target is Augustine's claim that sin is transmitted by begetting; keep generation vs imitation.
